transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Elaine (Redwood SE), Jonah (Redwood SE), Marcus (Zenith), Priya (Zenith), Luis (Zenith), Anya (Zenith)

Summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations for session-level prefix/KV caching and batching. Main goals: estimate cost savings vs hosted baseline, define pilot scope and required artifacts for a 24h throughput benchmark.

[00:00:00] Samir: ok hey everyone thanks for carving time, quick roll call?
[00:00:08] Marcus: hi Marcus here, platform lead at Zenith.
[00:00:11] Priya: Priya - eng manager.
[00:00:13] Luis: Luis - SRE.
[00:00:15] Anya: Anya, data science.
[00:00:18] Elaine: Elaine, solutions eng Redwood.
[00:00:20] Jonah: Jonah, performance SE.
[00:00:22] Samir: great quick agenda: 1) we show Optimize recommendations for batching & prefix/KV cache, 2) cost model and sample sims, 3) pilot scope and next steps. anything to add?
[00:00:30] Marcus: sounds good, main thing for us is whether we should go hosted for a month or do dedicated reserved capacity for pilot. also curious about session caching because our app keeps state per user.
[00:00:40] Samir: perfect. Elaine do you want to start with the caching sketch?
[00:00:44] Elaine: yeah sure. so at a high level Redwood Optimize looks at your session patterns and suggests two levers: prefix cache (we call it prefix but it's really a hashed session prefill), and KV cache which is a per-session kvstore for recurring tokens. the idea is to avoid re\u2011computing the same prompt prefix tokens on each request.
[00:01:02] Anya: when you say prefix cache is that like prompt templating or full context reuse?
[00:01:06] Elaine: both, depends on how deterministic your prefix is. if users mostly send the same system + user frontmatter we can keep an encoded prefix in memory and reuse the KV cache to skip the attention work. it's more effective when the prefix is large relative to the generated tokens.
[00:01:22] [00:01:22] Jonah: quick note: our instrumentation sometimes reads K-V cash in transcripts as "K V cash" so apologies for the transcription oddness, just the systems spit out KV as two tokens sometimes.
[00:01:30] Luis: heh noted. so what's the typical hit on latency if you put prefix in cache?
[00:01:36] Elaine: good q. in our internal benchmarks with 8k sequence models, a warm prefix cache can drop per\u2011request latency by 30–60% depending on token distribution because the runtime avoids re-running the full prefix attention. for short generation (<200 tokens) that's meaningful. for long tail outputs the marginal drop is smaller.
[00:01:54] Priya: and what about batching interplay? if I batch more to lower cost does caching cause batching inefficiencies?
[00:02:00] Jonah: tradeoff there. batching helps throughput but increases per\u2011user latency jitter because you wait to fill the batch or hit a timeout. prefix cache reduces compute per request, which lowers the incremental cost per token so you might be able to reduce batch sizes and still hit your cost targets. in other words caching and batching are complementary.
[00:02:20] Samir: let's walk a concrete Zenith example. Marcus you sent a session histogram earlier showing median session is 4 requests with average input prefix ~620 tokens and expected response ~120 tokens, right?
[00:02:29] Marcus: correct, though the tail has sessions up to 15 requests. we attached the CSV earlier.
[00:02:35] Elaine: OK using that distribution we ran a rough cost sim: baseline hosted (no cache) with 1.2k average prompt size yields about $0.045 per request compute-equivalent, adding prefix cache drops it to $0.017 per request when cache hit rate is ~70%. those are model-internal compute equivalents —  this doesn't include network egress or storage.
[00:02:58] Anya: 70% hit rate is optimistic, how sensitive is cost to hit rate?
[00:03:02] Jonah: very sensitive early on. at 40% hit rate the per-request cost is only down to $0.032. so we focus on how to increase hit rate: canonicalize templates, normalize user signals, and TTL tuning.
[00:03:16] [00:03:16] Luis: how do you canonicalize? we have examples where small date/time tokens or session-specific IDs break the prefix signature.
[00:03:22] Elaine: good point. we suggest two approaches: 1) client-side templating to replace ephemeral tokens with placeholders before sending, 2) server-side strip/normalize rules in the Redwood Console that run pre-hash. both are in the quickstart.
[00:03:36] Marcus: for private deployment we have stricter constraints — we need KMS integration and audit logs. does prefix/KV cache keep any PII?
[00:03:43] Elaine: cache entries are ephemeral by default and can be configured to be encrypted with your KMS if you run Private (VPC). For hosted we store caches in isolated tenant memory with optional retention controls and redaction hooks — the SOC2 docs cover this.
[00:03:58] Samir: here's the behavioral cost sim slide (shared link: https://app.redwood.ai/sim/znth-9-30).
[00:04:03] [00:04:03] Marcus: got it. looks like dedicated reduces base compute cost 20% but you have a fixed reserved monthly commit which we haven't decided on. pilot length will decide it.
[00:04:12] Jonah: for pilot we usually recommend hosted + Optimize tuning first, then if throughput or data-residency needs push to Dedicated or Private. pilot: 24h synthetic with your traces -> then evaluate cost per 1M session equivalents.
[00:04:25] Priya: what's involved in the 24h synthetic? do you need us to anonymize or can you run on our samples?
[00:04:30] Elaine: we accept anonymized corpora or you can run the benchmark in your VPC image — we provide a harness. minimal artifacts we need: sample prompt corpus, session arrival distribution, and QPS target.
[00:04:41] Anya: curious about batching config: you mentioned dynamic batching thresholds vs fixed batch sizes. how does Optimize pick those?
[00:04:47] Jonah: Optimize uses a cost+latency optimizer that simulates request arrival and selects a batch size and max latency (timeout) tradeoff. e.g., for your workload, a batch timeout of 8–12ms with max batch size of 16 gives good throughput while keeping p95 under 220ms for short responses. for larger models or longer responses you'll shift those numbers.
[00:05:06] Luis: 8–12ms wait seems tight, in our infra network jitter could be 5–20ms.
[00:05:10] Jonah: that's why we profile in your region. the harness includes a network jitter model. if your network has higher jitter we can raise the timeout and re-simulate cost impact.
[00:05:21] [00:05:21] Samir: we also calculate break-even for dedicated reserved vs hosted. quick note: for Zenith's projected QPS (peak 80 req/s sustained), dedicated becomes attractive if you commit to >500k sessions/month. below that hosted + Optimize tends to be cheaper.
[00:05:37] Marcus: our current monthly sessions are around 120k but we expect growth to 400k in 6 months. so borderline.
[00:05:44] Priya: in that case pilot should show how savings scale with adoption. do you simulate growth curves?
[00:05:49] Elaine: yes our cost model can simulate growth and show where reserved capacity beats hosted. we'll include a chart for the pilot.
[00:05:57] Anya: what about KV cache eviction and cold starts, do you have numbers?
[00:06:01] Jonah: eviction depends on footprint and TTL. in our runs a 200MB KV store per GPU with an LRU TTL of 48 hours gave >80% hit for stable session sets. cold starts for a missed prefix add the full prefix compute cost only on first request, subsequent requests are warm.
[00:06:18] Luis: how easy is it to instrument hit rate in Console? we need realtime ops metrics.
[00:06:22] Elaine: Console exposes per-model and per-route cache hit rate, token-savings, and per-token cost breakdowns by prefix vs generation. you can set alerts on p95 latency and hit rate drop.
[00:06:33] [00:06:33] Marcus: ok let's get granular — what do you need from us to run the benchmark and what will you deliver?
[00:06:38] Samir: we'll run a 24h synthetic in our hosted infra with two modes: 1) baseline (no cache + default batching), 2) optimize (prefix cache + tuned batching). inputs we need: your sample corpus (anonymized), arrival distribution, and a target p95 latency threshold. deliverables: cost spreadsheet with per-mode cost, hit-rate summary, trace-level latency histogram, and recommended pilot config (batching/timeouts/KV TTL).
[00:07:03] Marcus: timeline?
[00:07:05] Samir: if you send artifacts by Oct 2 we can run by Oct 3 and share Thursday Oct 3 results, or Oct 6 at latest.
[00:07:13] Priya: we'll aim for Oct 2.
[00:07:15] Elaine: also we'll attach a short how-to for doing the same test inside your VPC in case you want to run privately.
[00:07:22] [00:07:22] Anya: any pitfalls you often see?
[00:07:25] Jonah: two common gotchas: 1) inconsistent templating that reduces cache hits; 2) instrumenting tokenization mismatch — e.g., staff tokenization differences can change token counts and so cost sims diverge. we recommend you use our tokenizer docker that matches runtime.
[00:07:42] Luis: on security side, if we go Private we need KMS+HSM and a weekly audit digest. can you include that in the SOC2 package?
[00:07:49] Elaine: yes we'll include the Private deployment checklist and KMS integration notes.
[00:07:54] Samir: ok let's capture immediate next steps — Marcus will send corpus and histogram, Elaine will send SOC2 and private checklist, Samir & Jonah run 24h benchmark and share costs, and we reconvene after results to decide on dedicated commit or continue on hosted pilot.
[00:08:11] Marcus: sounds good. one last question — do you support session-level stickiness so cache follows a user across shards?
[00:08:17] Jonah: yes through our smart routing you can pin sessions to a shard for duration or use a global KV with cross-shard lookup. pinning reduces cross-node overhead at cost of capacity fragmentation. We'll include both options in the pilot config.
[00:08:30] Priya: perfect. thanks everyone.
[00:08:33] Samir: thanks — we'll send the meeting notes and next steps. end of call.

Notes on transcript quality: some speaker labels are approximate. There are occasional ASR errors (KV -> K V cash, KMS pronounced K M S).
